author: KERNAL Content Team
title: Ensemble Methods
subtitle: Bagging, boosting, Random Forest, and XGBoost

whyItExists.problem: Individual models (decision trees, linear models) have fundamental limitations — they either overfit (high variance) or underfit (high bias). No single model type dominates on all datasets.
whyItExists.solution: Ensemble methods combine multiple models whose errors are independent. When errors are uncorrelated, averaging predictions cancels them out, achieving better accuracy than any individual model.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When you need the best possible accuracy on structured/tabular data. Random Forest and XGBoost are the dominant approaches for most real-world ML competitions and production systems.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When you need a fully interpretable model (a single decision tree is better). Also when training time is severely constrained and a simple model suffices.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine asking 100 experts a question instead of one. Even if each expert is sometimes wrong, they tend to make different mistakes — so the majority vote is usually right. That's what ensemble methods do with ML models.
explainModes.simple: Bagging trains many models on different random samples of the data and averages their predictions. Boosting trains models one after another, each one focusing on the mistakes of the previous. Both produce much better results than a single model.
explainModes.standard: Bagging (Random Forest) reduces variance by averaging predictions of independent trees. Boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) reduces bias by sequentially fitting residuals. Both outperform single models on tabular data.
explainModes.technical: Random Forest uses bootstrap aggregation and random feature subsets to decorrelate trees, reducing variance without increasing bias. Gradient Boosting minimises a differentiable loss function by iteratively adding weak learners (trees) in gradient space.
explainModes.deepDive: The bias-variance decomposition explains why ensembles help: averaging B independent trees with variance σ² gives variance σ²/B. Correlated trees (ρ) limit the reduction: ρσ² + (1-ρ)σ²/B. Random feature subsets reduce ρ. Gradient Boosting solves loss minimisation in function space via steepest descent.

content.text: Ensembles combine multiple models to outperform any single model. The key insight: if models make independent errors, averaging their predictions cancels errors out. The two main strategies are bagging (parallel, reduces variance) and boosting (sequential, reduces bias).

Random Forest trains hundreds of decision trees, each on a random bootstrap sample of data and a random subset of features. Final predictions are made by majority vote (classification) or averaging (regression). The randomness makes trees independent, so their errors cancel.

content.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=200,      # number of trees
    max_depth=None,        # let trees grow deep (bagging handles variance)
    min_samples_leaf=2,
    max_features='sqrt',   # sqrt(n_features) per tree — key for decorrelation
    bootstrap=True,        # sample with replacement
    n_jobs=-1,             # parallel training
    random_state=42
)

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=skf, scoring='f1')
print(f'F1: {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}')

# Feature importances
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
importances = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns)
print(importances.sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))

content.text: XGBoost builds trees sequentially: each new tree focuses on the residual errors of the previous ones. It uses gradient descent in function space, which is why it's called 'gradient boosting'. XGBoost adds hardware optimisations and regularisation on top.

from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold

xgb = XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=500,
    learning_rate=0.05,    # smaller = more trees needed but better generalisation
    max_depth=6,
    subsample=0.8,         # row sampling per tree
    colsample_bytree=0.8,  # feature sampling per tree
    reg_alpha=0.1,         # L1 regularisation
    reg_lambda=1.0,        # L2 regularisation
    eval_metric='logloss',
    early_stopping_rounds=20,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Train with early stopping
xgb.fit(

from sklearn.ensemble import StackingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVC

# Level 0: diverse base models
base_models = [
    ('rf', RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)),
    ('gb', GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)),
    ('svm', SVC(probability=True, kernel='rbf'))
]

# Level 1: meta-learner combines base model predictions
stacking = StackingClassifier(
    estimators=base_models,
    final_estimator=LogisticRegression(),
    cv=5,         # use CV to generate training predictions for meta-learner
    stack_method='predict_proba'
)

stacking.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f'Stacking F1: {f1_score(y_test, stacking.predict(X_test)):.3f}')

a.name: Random Forest
a.description: Parallel ensemble — trains trees independently and averages
weaknesses: Often slightly less accurate than boosting
a.useWhen: You want a strong, reliable baseline with minimal tuning

b.name: XGBoost / LightGBM
b.description: Sequential ensemble — each tree corrects previous errors
strengths: Usually highest accuracy on tabular data
weaknesses: Slower on large datasets than LightGBM
b.useWhen: You need maximum accuracy and are willing to tune hyperparameters

content.text: XGBoost and LightGBM win most structured-data Kaggle competitions. Use them as a strong baseline. But start with Random Forest first — it requires almost no tuning and gives a good performance floor.

questions.question: What does Random Forest use to create diversity among trees?
options: Random bootstrap samples of data and random subsets of features
questions.explanation: Random Forest combines bootstrap sampling (random rows) and random feature subsets for each tree. This creates independent, decorrelated trees whose errors cancel when averaged.

questions.question: In gradient boosting, each new tree is trained to:
options: Fit the residual errors of the existing ensemble
questions.explanation: Boosting trains each tree to predict the residuals (errors) of the current ensemble. The new tree's predictions are added to the ensemble's predictions, correcting those errors.

questions.question: What does the learning_rate parameter control in XGBoost?
options: How much each new tree contributes to the final prediction
The maximum depth of each tree
The fraction of features used per tree
questions.explanation: Learning rate (also called eta) scales the contribution of each tree. Lower learning rate = each tree contributes less, requiring more trees (n_estimators), but typically improving generalisation.

faq.q: When should I use boosting vs bagging?
faq.a: Bagging (Random Forest) works well out of the box and is hard to overfit — good for a quick, reliable baseline. Boosting (XGBoost) is usually more accurate but needs careful tuning of learning_rate, n_estimators, and max_depth.

faq.q: Do I need to scale features for Random Forest or XGBoost?
faq.a: No. Both are tree-based algorithms that split on feature thresholds — the absolute scale doesn't matter. This is a big advantage over linear models and k-NN.

faq.q: What is the difference between XGBoost and LightGBM?
faq.a: Both are gradient boosting frameworks. LightGBM is significantly faster on large datasets because it grows trees leaf-wise (rather than level-wise) and uses histogram-based splitting. XGBoost is more established and sometimes more stable on small datasets.

examples: XGBoost for customer churn prediction — won multiple industry ML challenges
Random Forest for feature importance ranking in genomics studies
LightGBM for real-time ad click-through rate prediction at billions of rows
